fixes.row: Turn, and be forgiven, healed, saved, live
fixes.why: Two of the row's four shown examples (Matt 13:15, Mark 4:12) say the opposite of the label: the hearts are made callous 'otherwise they might turn and be forgiven' / 'turn, and I would heal them'. Under a heading that reads as a promise, a reader sees the verses as saying turn and be forgiven; they say the turning is what is withheld. Isa 6:10 and Acts 28:27 are the same text and sit in the row too. It is also the hardening text over which election readers part, so it should not stand as a plain example of the promise.
fixes.fix: Move Isa 6:10, Matt 13:15, Mark 4:12, Acts 28:27 out of this row into their own row, e.g. 'Lest they turn and be healed' (hearts made callous, 'otherwise they might turn'), with a note: the text says it of this people, the page does not say why or take a side on what it implies. Then the eg of this row are 2 Chr 7:14, Jas 5:20, Ezek 18:23 and Isa 55:7.

fixes.row: Repent and be baptized / Repent and believe / Turn, and be forgiven (verb) and A baptism of repentance / Repentance and forgiveness of sins / Repentance and faith (noun)
fixes.why: The notes say the page takes no order, but the row order says one. Verbs run forgiven, then baptized, then believe; nouns run baptism, then forgiveness, then faith. Read as steps, that is baptism before faith and forgiveness in the middle, a sacramental sequence a Baptist reader will see at once and a Reformed or Wesleyan reader will not accept. Any adjacent run of the three reads as a sequence. (The single-verse Acts 2:38 row itself is fine: it is the one sentence that has both words, and the note is balanced.)
fixes.fix: Order the three rows in each form by the canonical position of each row's first verse (verb: Repent and believe [Mark 1:15], then Turn and be forgiven, then Repent and be baptized [Acts 2:38]; noun: A baptism of repentance [Matt 3:11], Repentance and forgiveness, Repentance and faith), or better, do not leave them contiguous: put an unrelated row between each. Add one shared note to the first of each cluster: 'These rows are listed in the order of their first verse in the Bible. The page does not order repentance, baptism, faith and forgiveness.'

fixes.why: The label puts repenting first while the note says the page does not. One of the row's own verses (Acts 11:21) has them the other way, 'believed and turned', and Acts 26:18 has the turning and then 'faith in Me'. Readers who hold that faith comes first (or that repentance does) can each find their order in the label's wording and not in the other.
fixes.fix: Relabel 'Repent and believe; believed and turned' (Mark 1:15 and Acts 11:21 in the text's own words), keep the note.

fixes.row: Repent and believe; They did not repent, would not return
fixes.why: Matt 21:32 is μεταμέλομαι (regret, change one's mind), not μετανοέω. It is shown as an example of 'Repent and believe' (its lemma tag appears, but the row says repent) and also in 'They did not repent'. The hub's own rule is that μεταμέλομαι lives in the 'Regret, remorse, a change of mind' row, named as another word; here it is handed over as the same word as the other verbs.
fixes.fix: Remove Matt 21:32 from 'Repent and believe' and 'They did not repent' and leave it in 'Regret, remorse, a change of mind', where its word is named (the Berean's 'repent and believe him' stays visible there). Matt 21:32 then also drops out of the shown examples of 'Repent and believe'.

fixes.row: One sinner repents: joy in heaven; a brother repents, forgive him
fixes.why: The note says readers part on whether forgiveness waits for repenting, but the row shows only the conditional side ('if he repents, forgive him'), so a reader sees one side presented as the question's whole answer. The other side (forgiveness given with no repenting stated, e.g. Luke 23:34; Matt 18:21-22; Col 3:13) is not repentance's word and so is not here. Also two different claims (joy in heaven, forgive the brother) share one label, which can read as one cause.
fixes.fix: Keep the row. Rewrite the note: 'Luke 17:3-4 says forgive “if he repents”. Whether forgiveness waits for repenting is where readers part; verses that speak of forgiving with no mention of repenting are on forgiveness (link). The page takes no side.' Optionally split Luke 15:7, 15:10 (joy in heaven) from Luke 17:3-4 (forgive him) as two rows.

fixes.row: God grants repentance; kindness leads to it
fixes.why: (1) Rule 3: in Acts 5:31 the one who is to 'grant repentance' is the exalted 'Prince and Savior' (God exalted Him in order to grant), and the Greek does not settle whether the grantor is the Father or Jesus; the label says 'God grants' and files it by an inferred reading. (2) 2 Pet 3:9 is God's patience and wanting everyone to come to repentance, not 'kindness leads to it', yet it is the Wesleyan/Baptist key text and stands under that half of the label. One row with both halves is acceptable as two views side by side, but the label should say what the verses say.
fixes.fix: Relabel 'Repentance granted; God's kindness and patience lead to it', and let the note read: '“Grant repentance” and “everyone to come to repentance” stand side by side; in Acts 5:31 the text does not say who grants (the exalted Prince and Savior, or God who exalted Him). Where traditions part on how granting and a person's turning relate, the page takes no side.' Keep one row; splitting it would make the two views look like opposing camps.

fixes.row: Fruit and deeds in keeping with repentance
fixes.why: Heb 6:1 is 'repentance from dead works': the works repentance turns from, not fruit or deeds that keep with it. It is one of the row's four shown examples, so the label does not describe it. The note quotes it as one of the 'text's own phrases', which hides the difference, and the row is the faith-and-works row, where a misfiled verse tilts.
fixes.fix: Relabel 'Fruit and deeds in keeping with repentance; repentance from dead works', or move Heb 6:1 to 'Repentance and faith' only (where it already sits). Keep the note.

fixes.row: No ground for repentance, restored to repentance
fixes.why: Rule 1: the label 'restored to repentance' and the Heb 6:6 example text (which begins mid-sentence 'and then have fallen away - to be restored to repentance') omit the verse's governing word, 'impossible' (Heb 6:4). As shown, 'restored to repentance' reads as something the text offers. That softens a hard text and a reader on the free-grace side will see it as softened, while the other side will see the note's 'whether ... can be restored' as phrased to leave the door open. Heb 12:17 is said of Esau (Gen 27) and the label gives no hint of it.
fixes.fix: Relabel '“Impossible ... to be restored to repentance”; “no ground for repentance”' and show Heb 6:4-6 as the example (or add 6:4 to the row). Note: 'Heb 6:4-6 says it is impossible to restore again to repentance those who have fallen away; Heb 12:17 is said of Esau, who “could find no ground for repentance”. Where Christian traditions part on whether a believer can fall away and what this verse says of it, the page takes no side.'

fixes.why: Rule 1: these three do not say the LORD relents. Exod 32:12 is Moses asking ('Turn from Your fierce anger and relent'); Joel 2:14 and Jonah 3:9 are 'Who knows? He may turn and relent'. The note says they 'say the LORD “turns” (שׁוּב) from His anger beside the relenting', which is not what they say, and under the label they read as statements that He does. A classical-theist reader is right to object that an open possibility is filed as an event; the rabbi would point out the same in Jonah 3:9.
fixes.fix: Move Exod 32:12, Joel 2:14, Jonah 3:9 to a row of their own: 'Turn and relent: asked of the LORD, or hoped for' (note: Moses asks, the king and the prophet say “Who knows?”; the page does not say whether He did - see Jonah 3:10). Shorten the relents-row note to: 'A different word and sense from a person's repenting: נָחַם of the LORD. It is not a verdict on whether God changes; the next row has the verses where He does not.'

fixes.row: Every other use: turn, return, repent
fixes.why: The first example shown is Isa 57:6, 'Should I relent because of these?', the LORD relenting (נָחַם), under a label of 'turn, return, repent' and in a hub that insists God's relenting is another sense. A reader will see the LORD as 'repenting' here. Luke 22:32 ('when you have turned back') is Peter, an ordinary turn; both are real 'other uses' but the label does not cover Isa 57:6.
fixes.fix: Relabel 'Every other use: turn, return, repent, relent' and put the repentance uses (Luke 16:30, Jer 34:15, Luke 22:32, Zech 1:6) first in `eg`, so that Isa 57:6 is not what a reader sees first.

fixes.row: words (שׁוּב) and “Turn from wickedness, sin, idols, deeds; the repentant ones” / “Turn to the LORD, to God”
fixes.why: Rule 4: the hub counts 114 of שׁוּב's 953 uses and presents them under rows labelled 'repent', 'turn from sin', 'turn to the LORD' with the gloss 'to return: repent'. Nothing a reader sees says that שׁוּב is the ordinary Hebrew 'to turn, return' (home, back, restore, again), that the Hebrew Scriptures have no separate word 'repent', and that the 839 other uses are why 'return' is the root picture the prophets work with (return to the LORD, and He returns). The selection is sound; the reader is not told it was made. A rabbi seat will read 114 verses of selected 'repentance' and think שׁוּב has been narrowed to a Christian sense. This is the 'one sense presented as the whole' risk, here only in the missing disclosure.
fixes.fix: Show on the שׁוּב word line, from `other_sense` already in `words`: 'שׁוּב is the common Hebrew “turn, return, go back”; the text uses it of going home, restoring and repaying as well. These 114 verses are the ones where it is a turning to God or from sin; the other 839 are on the word's card.' Do not call it 'repent' in the gloss for שׁוּב alone: use 'to return: turn'. Keep the Hebrew rows first in order as built.

fixes.why: Rule 5: the four shown examples run NT, NT, OT, OT, so the first thing a reader meets under 'The call' is Mark 1:15 and Acts 3:19, and the Hebrew prophets' call (which the New Testament calls up) is second. The hub opens elsewhere on Isa 55:7, Ezek 18:23 and Joel 2:13, so the row is out of step with it.
fixes.fix: Set `lead` to Ezek.33.11, Joel.2.12, Mark.1.15, Acts.3.19 (Hebrew Scriptures first).

fixes.why: Luke 1:17 ('to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children') is a quotation of Mal 4:6 (3:24 in the Hebrew); the New Testament verse is in the hub and its Hebrew source is not, so the Hebrew Scripture appears only as the footnote to the Gospel.
fixes.fix: Add Mal 4:6 to this row (check the builder's versification, since Mal 4:6 has no original-language words in the Berean verse record) and keep the label.

fixes.row: What the text says of repentance (noun section)
fixes.why: The noun heading 'What the text says of repentance' reads as the text's whole account, but the noun rows are the Greek μετάνοια (24 verses, all New Testament except Isa 30:15); the Hebrew Scriptures' account of repentance is in the verb section. Said the other way, a reader coming for what the Hebrew Scriptures say could stop here and find only one verse.
fixes.fix: Retitle the noun section 'The noun “repentance”' (or 'Where the word “repentance” stands'), and the verb section can keep its title.

worker_points.point: 1. Baptism / forgiveness / faith rows; single-verse 'Repent and be baptized'
worker_points.why: The notes are balanced and a one-verse row is acceptable (it is the one sentence with both words, the text's own sentence, and the label does not interpret it). What tilts is the row order, not the single row; see the ordering fix. Nothing else singles Acts 2:38 out.

worker_points.point: 2. One sinner repents / a brother repents
worker_points.why: Fine as one row; the note should point to the verses on forgiveness where repenting is not mentioned, so the row does not look like the answer to whether forgiveness is conditional.

worker_points.point: 3. God grants repentance; kindness leads to it, one row or two
worker_points.why: One row reads as two views side by side, not one, so keep it. Fix the label for Acts 5:31 (who grants) and 2 Pet 3:9 (patience, not kindness).

worker_points.point: 4. No ground for repentance, restored to repentance
worker_points.why: The note takes no side but the label drops 'impossible'. Add 'impossible' and the Esau context.

worker_points.point: 5. Fruit and deeds in keeping with repentance (Heb 6:1)
worker_points.why: Heb 6:1 is 'repentance from dead works', which is not 'fruit in keeping with repentance'; relabel or move.

worker_points.point: 6. The LORD relents / does not relent side by side
worker_points.why: Fair to classical readers because the labels are the Berean's own words, they are set side by side with the 1 Sam 15 note, and the note says it is not a verdict. The only fix is the three verses (Exod 32:12, Joel 2:14, Jonah 3:9) that ask or hope rather than say the LORD relents. Also: 'does not relent' mixes statements of nature (Num 23:19, 1 Sam 15:29, Ps 110:4) with a stated resolve in one judgment (Ezek 24:14, Zech 8:14, Jer 4:28); that is accurate to the Berean and needs no change.

worker_points.point: 7. 'Turned to the Lord', to the Shepherd
worker_points.why: The label is the text's own words and the note refuses to pick Father or Christ, which is what rule 3 asks. Row 2 stays by-hand and names the LORD or God.

worker_points.point: 8. Unless you repent / if one does not repent
worker_points.why: The warnings are word for word and no verdict on 'perish' is given. Rev 2:5, 16, 22 are to churches and Luke 13:3, 5 to hearers of Jesus; the row does not claim they are one thing, and an added note would itself be a reading.
The label says nothing of who the Servant is; the Berean's 'bring Jacob back to Him' supports the inclusion. Only Mal 4:6 should be added next to Luke 1:17 (see fix).

worker_points.point: 10. Jewish teshuvah: only turning to God or from sin counted, 839 left out
worker_points.why: The selection by hand is the right one for a hub on repentance, and the main teshuvah texts (Deut 30, 1 Kgs 8, Isa 55, Jer 3-4, Ezek 18 and 33, Hos 14, Joel 2, Jonah 3, Mal 3:7) are in. But the reader is not told the other 839 exist or that the Hebrew has no separate word for 'repent'; add the statement on the word line. Also missing Deut 30:8 (see missing).

worker_points.point: Left out on purpose: turning away FROM the LORD (Ezek 18:24-26)
worker_points.why: Ezek 18 is the hub's centrepiece (six verses of it are in, and 18:23 is a key verse), and the half of the chapter in which a righteous man turns from his righteousness is left out. The reasons are sound for the rest of 'turning away', but on Ezek 18 the omission reads, to a Wesleyan or Pentecostal reader, as the hub avoiding the verses that cut against eternal security, and to a Reformed reader nothing changes by showing them. Show Ezek 18:24 and 18:26 in the 'Unless you repent' neighbourhood or add a one-line note that the chapter also has the righteous man turning away.

worker_points.point: Left out on purpose: the LORD's anger turning away (Ps 85:3 etc.)
worker_points.why: It is the LORD's side and the 'Turn and relent' verses carry what the pairing needs.

worker_points.point: Left out on purpose: other words (סוּר, הִתְוַדָּה, כָּנַע, ἐξομολογέομαι, στρέφω)
worker_points.why: Rule 4 forbids equating them; the hub's `others` is empty because none is rendered 'repent' enough. Their absence is a limit to mention, not a fault.

worker_points.point: What the builder could not express (items 1-7)
worker_points.why: These are builder limits, not reader-facing faults. Item 1 (a visible second list for the other uses of שׁוּב) is answered in part by the disclosure line in the fix on the word line.

missing.what: Deut 30:8 -- 'you will again obey' is the Hebrew שׁוּב ('you shall return and obey'), in the middle of the 30:1-10 passage whose 30:2 and 30:10 are in the hub. The Berean's 'again' hides the verb, so the gloss rule dropped it; the original has the turn, and it is the central teshuvah verse for Jewish readers.

Ezek 18:24 and 18:26 (and 33:18): a righteous man turns from his righteousness and dies. Ezek 18 is shown only on the wicked man's turning; the verses of the chapter that the Wesleyan, Pentecostal, Catholic and Orthodox readers cite are absent, which looks like selection. They are 'turn' (שׁוּב) with the same verb, set with a note that the page takes no side.

The LORD relenting toward His servants in compassion (נָחַם hithpael/niphal, rendered 'have compassion' or 'moved to pity' by the Berean and so dropped by the gloss rule): the 'relents' row has only relenting from disaster and regret, not the relenting that is pity, which the Hebrew Scriptures hold alongside it.

summary: The hub is faithful and carefully hand-selected, and its baptism, faith and forgiveness notes and its relents/does not relent pair take no side, but several labels and shown examples do not say what their verses say (Isa 6:10 and its quotations under 'Turn, and be forgiven', the 'impossible' missing from Heb 6, Exod 32:12/Joel 2:14/Jonah 3:9 under 'The LORD relents', Heb 6:1, Acts 5:31, Isa 57:6), and the row order reads as a baptism-faith sequence. The Hebrew Scriptures need a visible statement that שׁוּב is ordinary 'turn, return' and that 839 other uses were set aside, plus Deut 30:8 and Ezek 18:24-26 so that the selection does not look like a side.
